utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, will you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Good afternoon, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On this Thursday, the 27th of August, 2009, I bid good afternoon to Mr. Praljak, Mr. Prlic, Stojic, Petkovic, and Pusic, the ladies and gentlemen of the Defence counsel, Mr. Stringer, his assistant, and everyone else assisting us in the courtroom. We will complete this week with the cross-examination of Mr. Stringer on the basis of the binders, so I give the floor to Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good afternoon. Good afternoon, Your Honours, Counsel, everyone else in and around the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Good afternoon, General.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, if I could ask the usher to hand you the binder with the list, six documents in it, and I think we're getting toward the end of that binder, General. Yesterday, we were at Exhibit P03458. Do you have that, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And I was asking you questions about this document when we ended the proceedings yesterday, General. It's a report dated the 15th of July, 1993, from SIS chief in Tomislavgrad to the SIS Administration, and he's writing about the situation in Prozor. And in particular, he's writing about the crimes and the terrorising that's taking place in respect of the Muslim population in Prozor. Now, General, yesterday, when we completed or when we finished the proceedings, I was asking you about your responsibilities in respect of civilians in the areas such as -- in the areas that fell under HVO military control. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you were distinguishing or you were -- you were talking about your responsibilities, if I understand correctly, in respect of HVO front-line positions where you were conducting combat activities. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exact, I remember, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, I want to -- I want to get this clear before we move on to the next document. General, I'm going to put it to you that -- well, let me put it to you this way, because now we're talking about the 15th of July, 1993, and so we're talking about a period of time in which General Petkovic is the chief of the HVO Main Staff. He's the highest-ranking military person in the HVO; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: He is the highest-ranking person in the Main Staff and with respect to the units subordinated to the Main Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And at this time, 15 July 1993, you were commanding HVO units in the field in the Prozor area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. On the 15th of July, 1993, I was no longer in Herzegovina. With the completion of the operation in Boksevica, I returned to Zagreb until the 24th, when I took over duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And we've talked about the Boksevica operation already. On the 15th of July, 1993, General, tell us, since you came into your position as commander of the HVO Main Staff about nine days after the date of this document, do you consider that on the 15th of July, as chief of the HVO Main Staff, General Petkovic bore ultimate responsibility for protecting the civilian populations that were in areas controlled by the HVO military?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not, sir. That cannot be. That is not in accordance with the military rules, and it simply is not possible. The army cannot protect or be responsible for the territory outside the lines of responsibility; only if it appears as an occupation force, as in Iraq, for instance. But even then, you can see from that example, the example of Baghdad and the rest, the army is not responsible for half a million people that have been killed there. It's simply not possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, this report, General, is talking about Prozor, and it's talking about Muslims -- well, let me just read from part of it on the second page of the English: "They are taking from the Muslims gold, money, and more valuable --"

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I have a question to put to you, because I have been listening very carefully to what you are saying, and you put a question to General Praljak which seems to me to be a highly legal question. General Praljak answered on the basis of common sense without being familiar with the jurisprudence. Your question was, You're responsible for the civilians. Mr. Stringer, I would like to know on what juridical basis you're saying that. The accused tells you, I'm responsible for the zone of command, that is, within the military zone, and it seems to me, unless I'm mistaken, that in the jurisprudence of the Nuremberg trials concerning generals of the Wermacht, it was, in fact, stated that in the case of occupation, the general is responsible for the civilians, but in the occupied zones. So I would like us to be clear whether the Prosecution believes that in the case of a civil war, or any other form of war, the zone of command, of military command, implies a responsibility and competence over the fate of the civilians.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, it seems to me that we may be talking about two things, and the general has taken us off in a direction that's actually not the direction that I'm interested in. I'm not interested in the status of the HVO, whether it was an occupying force or not. I'm more interested in learning from the general what he believed to be his responsibilities or the responsibilities of his predecessor, General Petkovic, in terms of -- in not a legal sense, but a factual sense. A commander or a chief of the HVO Main Staff has a lot of things -- responsibilities that they are required to undertake, from a factual point of view. They command, they plan, they deploy. And I'm trying to ask the general about how he viewed -- whether there was, among those factual responsibilities of the commander, whether protection of civilians, the civilian population, against crime is among the responsibilities that fell to him. So that's where I'm trying to -- I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand better now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, let me try to break this down a little bit. This report's talking about crimes that are being committed against the Muslim population, mostly by the military policemen, as it says here. Now, can we agree -- well, let's assume that these Muslims are in an area in Prozor that is under the control of HVO armed forces, the HVO military. Okay? Can we agree on that for purposes of this discussion?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Stringer, Prozor was not under the control of the HVO forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I'm going to insist that you listen to my questions very closely and answer as precisely as you can. There was a part of Prozor that was under the control of the HVO armed forces; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Why do you expect me to tell you "under HVO control"? The HVO, in certain parts of Prozor municipality, had front-lines towards the Army of Republika Srpska in the west and certain front-lines towards the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and is responsible to keep order on those lines. If those lines are close to villages, in a village, or in front of a village, they're responsible to make sure that HVO troops, in those villages and in those houses, do not commit something that is contrary to war law, responsible in the sense that they must not issue such an order, that they must familiarise the troops with the Law of War, let them set an example by their behaviour. The rest is the responsibility of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Behind the front-line positions, the HVO's front-line positions, there were territories -- there were areas where Muslim civilians were living, and those areas were under the control of the HVO armed forces; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, they were not under the control of the HVO armed forces. Those people were deployed in 50 or 60 villages in the municipalities, and they lived, as far as Mostar goes, they lived there. And, of course, like all the citizens in the world, they were exposed to the possibility of theft, but they are not under the control of the army, which falls under the command of the Main Staff of the HVO. I'm telling you this crystal clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PRANDLER
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak -- I'm sorry, Mr. Stringer, to interrupt you. I really do not understand the situation. You mentioned in your previous answer that: "... the HVO, in certain parts of Prozor municipality, had front-lines towards the Army of Republika Srpska in the west and certain front-lines towards the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and is responsible to keep order on those lines. If those lines are close to a village or are close to villages, in a village, or in front of a village, they are responsible to make sure that HVO troops in those villages and in those houses do not commit something that is contrary to the war law, end of quotation. So now I really do not understand that -- at the same time, now again you say that you do not understand the situation, I mean, the question of the Prosecution, and you said that you do not have their -- you were not there to be responsible to keep order on those lines. So then what happened? Was there a vacuum? Were those territories really empty, there were no people, there were no -- any senior order? So, really, I believe that the questions which the Prosecution asked are to be answered. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour Judge Prandler, I don't know how what I said was interpreted. I said that along those lines, the HVO, or, rather, the Command of the HVO, is responsible, or, rather, the commander is responsible, and his superior, et cetera. I said that they are responsible for those lines. But the rear is hundreds of kilometres behind them, and for the whole depth of that territory outside the lines held by the troops and immediately behind the lines, the HVO is not responsible. As far as I know, not in any army or any law that I have read are they held responsible, except if --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Praljak. To assist in understanding this, because it's very complicated, let us imagine that we are in Prozor. We're going to transpose Prozor into this courtroom. Let us say that the HVO front-line goes from Mr. Karnavas, Mr. Khan, and Madam Nozica. That is the HVO lines, and where the Judges are is the front-line of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Does that mean that, according to what you say, that the civilians behind the front-line, Madam Alaburic, for instance, she's a civilian, she does not belong to the zone of responsibility of the HVO because she's outside the front-line? Is that what you wish to tell us?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite so, Judge Antonetti. There are civilian authorities, the civilian police. Of course, there's control over troops that may do something, but the commander is responsible for the front-line. You saw my document about a village of Pridris [phoen] which was at -- precisely on the front-line, and of course I said, Remove all the inhabitants, including livestock, because I'm responsible to protect their lives, which were in jeopardy because of the fighting. I was present there, so I moved the population of both ethnicities, including their cows, so that they wouldn't get killed in the fighting between the army and the HVO, and that is where the responsibility of the commander ceases. He cannot have control over 50 and even more than 50 villages behind him. As far as I am familiar with the rules, the answer is "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have understood your answer. I give the floor to my colleague.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I just want to take another aspect, Mr. Praljak. The troops of the HVO under the General Staff were divided in operational zones, operation zones, not in lines. The zone is a surface which was -- you could draw on that map the limits of a zone. It was described as an area, not as a line; is that wrong?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is wrong. The zones here indicate -- when the front-lines are drawn, then you say up to this point on this line, usually one says, Including such and such an elevation point, including such and such a crossroads. Then the defence line goes on. Then there's the commander of that defence line. Usually, such a zone, such a line, is given to a battalion, as the smallest unit. Then the brigade has its own front-line, then Siljeg has his own front-line, and that's how this is done. These are not zones, as a territory, but precisely up to a certain point. Up to this village, such and such is in command, and then as the front-line goes on to the next table, someone else is in command of that front-line. So it's not a zone that consists of I don't know how many square kilometres behind the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I still don't take it that it is a line, Mr. Praljak. There is a line. Of course, I do not question that. But then to support that line, other military institutions are necessary. For instance, the artillery is a certain distance behind the line, perhaps several kilometres. There are logistic needs. There are depots of MTS that are placed behind the lines. So it is an absurd idea that the -- mathematically what the army is doing is holding a line like something you can draw with a pencil once from right to left, or vice versa. You have given us a conception here which is not convincing at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can only present what is written in all the rules of war. That's not my conception; that is how it functions. A gun that may be behind a hill certainly is linked by some sort of observation points and belongs to that operational zone, but the guns or the mortars are not positioned where there are people. A howitzer may be put somewhere in isolation behind a hill.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Mindua has a question to put.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, excuse me. Mr. Witness, in many international laws, when a state of war is declared on the territory of a state or a province or a locality, the political authority may decide to replace civilian authorities for that territory by military authorities. So the question I ask myself: With respect to these operational zones behind the front-lines, according to your own experience when you were on the front-line, or within your operational zone, the civilian authorities, did they continue to function? I'm talking about municipal authorities, civilian tribunals, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, all the structures of civilian authorities were operational in all the municipalities which were behind the front-lines held by the HVO, be it facing the Army of Republika Srpska or the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina when the conflict started. It is true, Your Honour, that when you're capturing a territory, for a certain amount of time until some sort of civilian authority is established by protectorate or, as we know from the history of warfare, by the English, for instance, for a time the commander of the army that has captured the territory is also responsible for that territory. But we were not conquering territory. This was not conquered territory. The civilian authority was functioning in all the municipalities in those territories, fully functioning. Whether they were functioning well or not so well, in view of the conditions, I don't think that is the subject of my testimony. But there was the mayor, the civilian police, and all structures of the civilian authorities.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. My last question on this issue: You said "behind the front-line." According to you, behind, that would be how far behind; a certain number of metres or kilometres? What is the distance that you mean when you're talking about the area behind the front-line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That distance of possible control depends on the terrain. If you are on certain lines and there's a small hill behind you, then, of course, you will position, at the very beginning of your line, certain guards so somebody would not be able to reach you from behind. It can be 200 metres, 300 metres. It depends on the configuration of the terrain, so that you couldn't be surprised by somebody hitting you from the back, but only in the military sense, in terms of protecting your own troops from a breakthrough of any small enemy unit from the rear which might kill your soldiers. And this happened in Capljina, when 26 men were killed well within the rear, if you remember that document, or the killing of those cooks that we discussed, and photographs were shown, when the ABiH killed them, 10 or 15 kilometres into the rear, when I got those fighters planes up because these were infiltrated territories to groups that can kill soldiers. Then the situation is different.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you very much. So my understanding is that this may vary between 200 metres to 15 kilometres, when you referred to the killing of HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, you can't control 15 kilometres of territory. They simply broke through. This can happen. You can penetrate hundreds of kilometres within -- most frequently, there was no protection behind the front-lines. Shall we say 100 metres, 50 metres? It depends on the assessment of the commander as to the possibility of a breakthrough from behind exists or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Praljak, you speak about a breakthrough behind. Breaking through what? If there is no HVO, there is no breaking through. They can go for a walk. HVO apparently, according to you, does not control the hinterland, it's got nothing to do with it. That is what is not very convincing, I must say.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot change your opinion about whether it's convincing or not. I claim that this is written in any army rules. The commander in the field may control a certain road, 100 metres or 50 metres, before his front-line, and he may position two guards on that road so that no one can reach them from behind. This is just control of his front-lines, not control of the territory. You cannot control the territory with an army. That is absurd. The fact that there may be an anti-air battery in an English town that will hit German bombers, that doesn't mean that the army is controlling the entire territory of England, because there are civilian authorities there. I'm sorry, I do know a little about wars.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think it's not necessary to repeat more. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour and Mr. President. Mr. President, what I'm going to do, although very much staying with this very issue - I don't want to give any indication that I'm moving to something different - I do want to move to the next document which I think will probably facilitate our questioning on this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I was waiting for my learned friend to end, since he said he was moving on to another document. For the sake of the transcript, to make sure that everything is clear later. When we get back to it, I'd like to say the following: We haven't so far objected to the use of this document and the Prosecutor using this document in his cross-examination. We didn't object because we didn't want to appear to be assisting the witness, but I think it is now my duty to say the following for the sake of the transcript. When my learned friend from the Prosecution asked Mr. Praljak yesterday, at the very beginning when dealing with this document, it was page 91, line 5 -- I apologise, it was before page 91. The question is a fairly lengthy one. When this question was put to the witness, the witness immediately replied that he had never seen the document before and that he knew nothing about it. In spite of that fact, an entire series of questions continued to be put to the witness about the document. The document, itself, as you have seen, gives no basis for the Prosecution to continue putting questions about it to the witness. The witness said, No, I have never seen the document. He also added that he had never been there, he wasn't there at the time, in fact. And the document also doesn't show that the document was supposed to be provided with the document. It wasn't addressed to him. It wasn't sent to him. And as a result, there is no basis to put questions to the witness about the document. This Chamber has respected that principle, and for the three and a half years that we have spent in this courtroom this Chamber has said that questions couldn't be put to a witness once the witness had said that he or she hadn't seen the document or hadn't been in the place concerned. The Prosecution has somewhat changed the approach today, and they are now proceeding by using hypotheses, If such and such a thing occurred, and so on and so forth. But this doesn't change anything. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Kovacic, the Chamber certainly does not agree with you, because, in fact, you are right when you say that Mr. Praljak isn't familiar with this document. On the 15th of July, as he, himself, said, he had returned to Zagreb. Fine. So it's difficult for him to answer questions about very precise facts. But, in fact, you saw that when the Prosecution put questions to the witness, well, it was interesting, because I discovered that there was the problem of the operative zone. I innocently thought that the operative zone covered a geographical area, but Mr. Praljak is claiming, and he says that this is supported by military rules and regulations, Mr. Praljak is claiming that the operative zone only covers the zone that the army is occupying as part of the front-line. And the Prosecution has put basic questions to him that concern principles. They've been using this document. They could have taken a different document. In the Prosecution's opinion, the HVO commander had a certain amount of responsibility for civilians or was responsible for civilians. If there is looting, if someone is killed, and so on and so forth, the issue of responsibility arises. So this document is being used, but in relation to principles. In relation to such principles, General Praljak has said that from his point of view, his responsibility is for the zone, the operative zone, and the civilian authorities are responsible for everything else. So your objection is interesting, but it in general terms it wasn't pertinent because questions could have been put with reference to other documents because we're now dealing with principles. So please do continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I think a correction imposes itself. It says in the transcript his responsibility -- Mr. Praljak said that his responsibility is for the zone, but I think that you say your responsibility is for the front-line, which is not the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak, your responsibility is for the front-line; that is to say, the zone covered by the front-line, even if it's only a few metres or a few hundred metres. That's all you're responsible for? You're not responsible for the hinterland?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct. The line -- the front-line, the zone, it's the same in this case. That's what it's called.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We have understood that. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to follow up on a little bit of this. General, it's absurd, isn't it, to suggest that the military commanders -- your only responsibility as a military commander was for the small area of the front-line, and that you, as the commander of the HVO Main Staff, bore no responsibility for the areas under HVO military control behind the front-line position? That's an absurd proposition, isn't it, one that you're advancing only to escape responsibility for the crimes that committed in those -- that were committed in those areas under HVO control; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not, Mr. Stringer. If your theory were applicable, 150 high-ranking American officers would be here because they were unable to control the situation in Iraq that they had taken by military force. These are well-known facts today. What controlling something means is well known. When they established a government over there, well, what are they responsible for? Are they responsible for who's being killed there?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Furthermore, your description now of what the area of responsibility of an operative zone is equally absurd, where you claim that the operative zone consists only of the front-line areas and not the hinterlands or areas under HVO control that fall behind those front-line positions; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, if we're developing new theories and new rules, new laws about what this means, well, there's nothing I can add. It's obvious that one is trying to introduce completely new rules on warfare, on the rights that an army has, on the responsibility of a commander. But we keep talking about these matters, but we don't refer to any rule books, to any laws, to any examples of warfare in order to support the claims made by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, although General Praljak has already answered this question, I would like to object to the previous two questions put by my learned friend Mr. Stringer, and for the following reasons: Mr. Stringer has been asking whether a theory is absurd or not, and he is asking General Praljak to answer a question put in that way. But Mr. Stringer didn't say why it would be absurd if a commander was responsible for a front-line and the civilian authorities were responsible for the territory or some other community, so I believe that examining or cross-examining the witness in this manner is inappropriate. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I respectfully disagree with counsel. I propose to continue to the next document, although we are going to stay with this issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next document is P04177. Maybe this one's a better one for us to talk about, because it's made during the period of time after you have taken command of the HVO Main Staff. It's dated 14 August 1993. It's a report of Luka Markesic to the SIS of the HZ-HB in Mostar. And before we come back to these issues we've been discussing, let's go through the exhibit, and we'll talk about the factual situation on the ground there in Prozor in mid-August of 1993. Now, on page 2 of the English, General, for you it would be the paragraph under the name of Ante Pavlovic. There's a reference to the new commander, Ante Pavlovic. Do you see that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I object. I have an objection. I believe that before the Prosecution asks questions about this document, he must first establish whether the witness has seen the document, whether he knows anything about the document, and only then can he proceed, if the witness first gives him a basis to do so. Otherwise, he can use the document as an example of the events, which is what he did with the previous document to a certain extent. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm a bit surprised by this type of an objection, frankly, Mr. President. This is a factual account of the situation in Prozor in mid-August. The general's the commander of the HVO Main Staff at the time. We know that he, based on his own testimony, has made this particular area one of his top priorities, as commander, and that he spent a good deal of his time in this area. I'm going to go through this document with the general. We're going to establish his knowledge of the events that are taking place in this area, and on the basis of that we're going to continue with the discussion about what he believes he was or was not responsible for in respect of the crimes that were being committed by the Muslims in this area. The document will also show us that, in fact, General Praljak was in this area at the very time the document was written and that he was in the field using military or civilian police units in combat operations. So it's entirely appropriate to ask him questions about the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I don't see the problem. I've listened to Mr. Kovacic, and having listened to both of you, I was wondering something about the matter with regard to Article 7(3) of the Statute. If crimes have been committed, if something can be described as a crime, then the superior is responsible pursuant to Article 7(3). However, there are certain conditions. It's necessary that he was aware of the crimes, and so on and so forth. If you move into this area, however, it's necessary to ask Mr. Praljak, first of all, whether he was the HVO commander on the 14th of August. Answer, Yes. Then, secondly, Were you familiar with this document, yes or no? We don't know. If he says, Yes, you continue. If he says, No, you ask him, Why not? And then once he tells you, for example, I'm not familiar with this, then you can ask him about that. However, he said, with regard to the document, that if he says that such and such a thing happened, ask him whether he was familiar with it, and so on and so forth, because now everything you're dealing with falls under Article 7(3).

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, with respect, Mr. President, I would suggest -- or the position is that this is not limited to 7(3). This could very well go to Article 7(1), as well as JCE issues, so I don't agree with the limitation that's being suggested. Now, it is a common practice - it happens routinely and regularly - that witnesses are shown documents that they may not have seen before. They're asked whether the activities or the events described in the documents are consistent with what their understanding of the situation was or whether they knew about this, and that's precisely what the intention is going to be. So, Mr. President, I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, I totally agree with you, but I'm telling you, if we're dealing with a joint criminal enter prize, well, if there is no support for such an enterprise, nothing falls under 7(1), then we have Article 7(3) in the indictment. So if you don't want to cover the entire field, well, it's up to you to take such risks. But from a technical point of view, it's best to cover the entire field, to deal with all the aspects. But you're right, it's not necessary for the accused to be familiar with this document. You're perfectly right about that. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, with your leave, I fully agree with what you have said. If I may. The witness doesn't have to be familiar with the document. I fully agree with that. However, it's necessary for this to be established through the cross-examination, regardless of whether it falls under 7(1) or 7(3) or the category of joint criminal enterprise. If the Prosecution now examines the witness with regard to facts referred to in the document, well, this is how we have proceeded so far. First, it is necessary to establish whether the witness has seen the document, and then he can continue to ask questions about whether the witness knew anything about the events themselves, even if he didn't -- hadn't seen the document. I know I'm objecting in this case, because when you have a look at the title in the document, when you have a look at the stamp, you can see that this has nothing to do with the staff, and the Prosecutor's fully aware of this. We can see who is writing to whom here, and we can't see a copy being addressed to the witness. So I do agree with you that then the Prosecution can ask any questions he likes, but first we have to establish what the link is between the witness and this document. Does the witness know anything about the document? We can then proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kovacic, the Prosecution has already asked questions about Prozor. Secondly, he has already asked questions on the basis of the SIS document. Thirdly, the author of this document, well, we've already seen documents drafted by this author, Luka Markesic. So there are a series of documents, a series of items that have already been seen and examined. This is an additional document that covers the period of August. We've already dealt with previous periods. So there is a line of conduct. We know what the basis is already. The Prosecution wants to know whether Mr. Praljak was familiar with what had happened in August in Prozor, et cetera, but an entire series of documents have demonstrated that certain things were occurring during the previous months. Please continue, Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may -- if I may add a question to Mr. Stringer. I do not quite see, I confess, what obstacle to your work it would be if you asked the witness has he seen this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I was going to do it, Mr. President -- or Judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, this is a report, as we've indicated, of Luka Markesic, who we talked about a number of times, directed to the SIS of the HZ-HB in Mostar. Did you see this document on or after the 14th of August, 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. On the 14th of August, I know for sure that I was in combat in the south of Mostar, and afterwards I didn't see the document, not until I arrived here as an accused.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the document does talk about a number of events in Prozor that I want to ask you about, ask you whether you had knowledge that these sorts of things were taking place. On page 2 of the English, after the reference to the new commander, Ante Pavlovic, Markesic writes about the fall of Konjic, Bugojno, and part of Gornji Vakuf, and he's talking about the refugees, women and children, elderly, who came from those places down to Prozor. And then he writes that: "Initially they," referring to the refugees, "were put up in Croatian houses, but when the number grew, they began to be settled in Muslim houses and villages. Thus, the entire Muslim population from Rama municipality is accommodated in three collection centres, Pograde, Duge, and Lapcanje [phoen]. "The relocation of these Muslims was done by the military police under the command of Ilija Franjic." Now, first question, General. Were you aware of the relocation of Muslims from Prozor, from their houses, to these collection centres to make room for incoming Croat refugees?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware that, as indicated here, the HVO military police was ordering Muslims to be evacuated or taken out of their houses and put in collection centres?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, Markesic continues to say that: "The arrival of soldiers and civilians into the municipality has caused an increase in crime, prostitution, the removal of Muslims from prison and their liquidation, the extortion of gold, money, and other valuables from Muslims, and liquidation after extortion." Now, just so we're clear with interpretation or translation issues, General, can we agree or would you agree with me when I suggest to you that when Markesic writes about liquidation here, he's talking about killing, people being killed?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's probably what he's talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: He continues on, I'm moving to the next page of the English: "Men also go to Muslim houses, and daughters are stripped naked in front of their fathers, and vice versa. All of this has been happening systematically for a considerable time now, even though we informed the HVO president, Mijo Jozic, the brigade commander, and the commanders of the military and civilian police of this in writing." And then he goes on to say that he's enclosing reports from the prison warden, and he's also enclosing statements of Muslim women who have been raped. He says: "Such things are mostly done by local soldiers and some of the military police. Thus, the Security Service is unable to deal with all matters because collaboration with military police concerning the prevention of such things is impossible, given that there are perpetrators among them. For now, we are succeeding in gathering information on the above matters, putting pressure on the Command and Presidency of the HVO to make sure these kinds of things are stopped." I'm going to skip a paragraph. He says: "The military police are implementing an order from a higher level to detain Muslims between the ages of 16 and 60 in their own particular way, imprisoning men without exception, including those younger than 16 and older than 60, and treating them in an extremely inhumane manner." I'm going to move to the next page in English. I'm going to skip a paragraph or two. He says that: "It has been known for some time that members of the military police have been involved in the seizure of vehicles from humanitarian aid convoys and that these vehicles are sold on the open market. The military police commander openly admits that he authorised the plunder of the convoy." Continuing down a few paragraphs, it says: "It should be noted that the military police go into the field every day on assault operations, and so the credit they attain in action among the people is wasted in the above deeds. As regards concrete cases, we have rationale for them. It is just that the times are such that it is dangerous to expound them." He goes on, in the next paragraph, to talk about how this affects morale, and then he says: "The civilian police are unable to cope with all this, and recently they have been mostly in the field under the command of General Slobodan Praljak." So, General, this document raises a number of topics that I'd like to ask you about. Would you agree with me, General, that assuming Markesic is accurately reporting the situation, the military police in Prozor are out of control in August of 1993?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't comment. I can't say anything more than what is written here. I can't say anything about whether it's true or not. I'm not familiar with the document. All I can do is repeat what I have already said with regard to this period from the 24th -- I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to repeat what you've already said, General. I'm asking you whether, as someone who's the commander of the HVO Main Staff at this period of time, whether, in your opinion, the HVO military police in Prozor was out of control.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: As you have seen in that sentence, the military police, when used in combat, fought well. And then he says the credit that they earned, when defending that area, was spent on these things. He continues to say all of this has an influence on the morale of many members of the Rama Brigade and on the people. So many of the people -- many soldiers don't agree with this, and their morale is undermined through such acts. When the military police was at the front-line, they were naturally under the command of that part of the front-line, and then that brigade, and then the operative zone, and then Praljak -- or Praljak when he was in the field, and then they fought well.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let's talk about that. These military police units, you've told us extensively in your testimony that you used them yourself, personally, in combat operations. The fact is, General, that you turned a blind eye to these crimes that they were committing because you wanted to continue to have them with you in the field in combat operations. That's the choice you made, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer, I didn't turn a blind eye to anything, never. The fighting up there, and I'll repeat this for the 10th, 20th, or 30th time, the fighting was so intense that --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you knew about all of this criminal activities of the HVO military police in Prozor and you did nothing about it; isn't that a fact?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So you're claiming that you didn't know about any of this, any of these crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about these crimes for the simple reason that no one informed me of them. And given the workload I had in combat, I don't remember having ever slept in the same bed on more than one occasion. So if you want to depict me, Commander of the Main Staff, as a god who could oversee everything and who was responsible for everything, well, you can do whatever you like, but that's not correct. I wanted to describe the wartime situation for you. You say that this was something that was known. The person who knows about this had the duty of filing criminal reports. That was his duty. No one, apart from him, had that duty. It was his duty to take action in order to charge these peoples.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, let's not waste time, let's not waste any more time. You haven't seen this document. Fine. The Prosecution is saying, Were you familiar with this? You said, No, I wasn't. Fine. Now I have a question I'd like to put to you, but from a different point of view. Let's imagine that at the time you found out that on the 14th of August, in Prozor, all these events took place. What would you have done?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Regarding the killing of this man, I would tell him that he must file criminal reports, that is his duty, that he should call on his superiors to arrest those people, because that is their duty, and that he should carry out his duty according to the laws and regulations, according to the line of subordination. That is what I would ask of the man writing the report, that he shouldn't write a report but that he should act in accordance with his official duty, because I personally cannot arrest anyone. That is not my job. I'm not responsible for the military police, nor do I have the ability to discover. It's like seeing a house burning and you have to find out who set fire to it. I simply don't understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say that the document reached the Defence Department on the 18th of August, number 693. There's a stamp on it, the receivable stamp. To the best of your recollection, did Mr. Stojic at some point tell you the following: General Praljak, we have had a whole series of reports regarding flagrant crimes, certain very serious offences being committed. What can the army do to assist the military police, the military prosecutor, the civilian police? Did you at some time have a conversation of this kind with Mr. Stojic, or did you not have any conversations about this issue?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not discuss this topic with Mr. Stojic.

utterances.speaker: MS. NOZICA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, with your permission. This is not an objection. Of course, there is no place for an objection. I asked for the witness to answer, but I think for this hypothesis which the President presented, we need to know that this -- whether this report reached Mr. Stojic at all or whether he was familiar with it. The stamp says that the report reached the SIS, and according to the number of the protocol we cannot see that this is a protocol number of the Defence Department, where Mr. Stojic was. And as there were questions as to whether Mr. Praljak was aware of this document, I wish to say for the transcript that from the stamp we cannot claim that Mr. Stojic was aware of this document either. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is just a possibility that I envisaged, and the emphatic reply by Mr. Praljak may also cover the fact that Mr. Stojic was not aware of it. That is quite logical. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, would you agree with me that in August of 1993, the head of the SIS for the HZ-HB was Mr. Lucic?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. According all -- according to all the information I have, it was Mr. Ivo Lucic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And he was a part of the HVO Defence Department; is that also correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to my information, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. Now, General, getting back to the document and the situation in Prozor, it seems to me, General, that you're forgetting what your position was on the 14th of August, 1993. You may have wanted to give yourself the luxury of just getting involved in specific combat operations and limiting your focus only to that, but the fact is, General, that when you agreed to take command of the HVO Main Staff, you assumed a greater scope of responsibilities than just a specific combat operation here or there. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which? Could you please tell me, on the basis of any document, what are the responsibilities of the commander of the Main Staff? Then we can discuss it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's talk about the responsibilities that flow to you as the superior of the commander of the operative zone, for example. The fact is that everything under that chain of command flows up to you and down from you through the operative zone, where all of this is taking place. Isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, this was not happening in the operative zone, but in the territory of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Excuse me, General. Isn't this -- isn't Prozor within the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone, and weren't these military police units here subordinated to the operative zone when you use them in these combat operations?

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I object to this question because I think it needs to be explained. It is not possible to subordinate a unit to an operative zone, because it is a territorial community, but it is subordinated to a particular commander. So I don't think the question is precise enough, and that is why General Praljak cannot answer it. Subordination must always be to a certain commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I think the general knows precisely what I'm talking about, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, you want to know what your responsibilities are. Evidently, you don't know what your responsibilities are, as commander of the HVO Main Staff? Is this where we're going to -- is this where our conversation's going? You want me to tell you what your responsibilities were?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, Mr. Stringer. I know perfectly well what my responsibilities are, but I think that either you know nothing about the army or you're making up things or a special case of responsibility for the HVO that does not apply to the American Army, nor the British, nor the French. That's what I think. I think you're making up something, and this wouldn't be a good idea.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Your position is that even though you're commander of the HVO Main Staff, and you're therefore the superior officer of your operative zone commander, Siljeg here, that really your only responsibilities are limited to the precise combat locations and activities that you're involved in on a day-to-day basis? Is that how we're to understand your testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is responsibility. When a unit has been mobilised and gathered at a certain position, when it is armed, loaded onto trucks and buses and moves on, then it becomes a part of the military, and command and responsibility over it begins. It is deployed to a certain position, subordinated to a commander, deployed in trenches or bunkers, and that is the responsibility of the commander from the bottom to the top.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: These military police units that are being referred to here that are involved in the combat operations in which they're able to distinguish themselves -- let me just read this passage to you again. Markesic writes: "It should be noted that the military police go into the field every day on assault operations, and so the credit they attain in action among the people is wasted in the above deeds." Now, General, I think we can agree, based on your extensive testimony on this, that those military police in the field on assault operations are subordinated to the operative zone, or the brigade, for operational purposes at that time; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. From a certain point in time, it is clearly stated to what commander they are subordinated, for what period, and what their assignment is. Once this ceases, they are no longer subordinated to that commander, and they are not accountable to the commander once their re-subordination ends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And you testified at one point early in your direct examination that even though they were subordinated to the operative zone for this purpose, they remained military police officers, they still remained within the structure of the Military Police Administration; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, the military police that are being referred to here appear to be involved in combat operations during the day and involved in criminal operations at night or when they're off duty, so the fact is that the operative zone, where the commander is using these military units in the field, are clearly responsible for these military police officers when they're committing crimes when they're off duty; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is not true. They didn't go to the front one day and then come back at night, but it is stated here that the Muslim offensive had calmed down on the 14th, and that is why I left the area. At the time, the military police -- will you let me answer your question? I told you the time has to be determined, to whom they are subordinated, with what aim, and until when? It's not for two hours, but a precise order has to be issued.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And during the period of that subordination, you're telling us that nobody is responsible for them if they commit crimes?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: When they are re-subordinated, they are accountable to their commander. But when irregularities have been established, sanctioning is done by the structure to which they belong. The commander, if he finds out, is duty-bound to report it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So these military police who are being referred to here, then, you're telling us that while they're subordinated to the operative zone, the operative zone people can't do anything to hold them accountable or to prevent them from committing more crimes; it's only the Military Police Administration that can take action after they're re-subordinated?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It depends on the type of offence. If a commander was present and the offence was murder, it is his duty to disarm him and arrest him. But as for other offences, he reports to the superior commander, who will then take steps against the offenders; an investigation, proceedings, et cetera. This is then passed on to other institutions, as anywhere else in the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, General, you're describing a very nice, tidy procedure which, in fact, no one was interested in, because your only interest was in using these military police units in combat activities, and you weren't interested in punishing them or doing anything other than using them in combat; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is not true, Mr. Stringer. I cannot do something about something I'm not aware of. And when the time -- the energy required -- you have an operation ongoing and someone does something somewhere, and if you're operating somebody's heart, you will stop that and investigate. You cannot understand the problem until the strength of the Muslim offensive at that point in time is recognised. And 15.000 to 20.000 refugees from Bugojno with the army, it is impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, you know about the refugees from Bugojno, General. The fact is that you know very well what the situation in Prozor was. You know that all the civilians had been moved out into these detention centres to make room for incoming Croat refugees. You knew that the Muslims were being terrorised, raped, liquidated. But the fact is you weren't interested in doing anything about all of that. You were only interested in conducting combat activities; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You're making things up, Mr. Stringer. It is -- what you are saying is absolutely not true, and you have been repeating it for the 50th time and you're angry if I tell you for the 50th time that that is not true, that the situation was not the way you describe it. Look at the next document and you'll see.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: This is what you said in your testimony on the 12th of May this year, very early in your direct examination. You were talking about using the military police, and you said: "I said very precisely that such a use of the military police will significantly decrease the ability of the military police to perform their tasks, their normal tasks, and that for that reason there will be an increase in the rate of general crime, and there will also be a decrease in the number of those who will be arrested for those crimes." Do you remember that testimony?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, that is what I said.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And so what you're telling us is you made a choice, a conscious decision, to use military police units in combat activities, knowing that this was likely to result in crimes such as we're seeing here in this document directed against the civilian population; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: My choice was a conscious, reasonable, rational one. I still stand by it, because that would have been done by any commander, every commander, whoever he may be, even if he is American. The main aim is to prevent the fall and the defeat that would have happened if I hadn't done this. And my knowledge, like that of any man, when the -- use the police from New York for something, there is no electricity or something, there will be a thousand crimes because people are thieves and murderers, at least a large number of them, and there's nothing you can do. But that doesn't mean that you will let the Japanese defeat you rather than using the police to prevent that. So please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: In terms of the justification for your decisions, it actually goes deeper than that, doesn't it, because you needed these military police units to fight, and you knew that if you punished them, put them in jail, removed them so that they could not continue to prey on the civilian population, you'd lose good fighters, and so you choose to keep the fighters and to tolerate the crimes that they were committing; isn't that so?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I refuse -- MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Please let me. Just a brief objection. The Prosecutor keeps using the term "military police units." I have kept quiet, but he's used this term so often that one would think these may be military police brigades. In this document, nor in any other, have we seen the term "units." These were cases, individuals, military policemen. There may have been five or six such offenders, or two of them. We don't know how many from these documents. We don't know who they were, what their names were, know how many of them there were. The concept of a unit does not exist. If the Prosecutor knows which units were involved, then let him tell us. I know which unit we are talking about, it was such and such a unit, and then we can proceed. There is absolutely -- it's not right to use the term "units." If anyone knows what units are involved, they should tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Furthermore, I want to say that the enormous number -- the majority, as everywhere else, the majority of military policemen were honest people of integrity who fought with honour and carried out their duties with honour. According to the logic of statistics, one could expect more offences, as I had said, but killed and wounded policemen who fought well were in the vast majority.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll come back to this when I come to my questions, but I'd rather let Mr. Stringer finish his questions first.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Just to respond briefly to counsel, we're talking about P04177. I'm talking about the crimes and the military police that are referred to in this document. Mr. President, I have just about exhausted my questioning on this document, so I think I can yield to the Trial Chamber if there are more.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, I have several questions. I am looking at this report by Luka Markesic, and there's nothing in it that would lead me to believe that it does not reflect the precise situation. There are many details there, and this is -- I believe that this is a situation as is described. And reading this report, I note that there are six persons whose role needs to be examined. This report refers to the president of the HVO of Prozor. The second person is the brigade commander. The third person who has a role is the commander of the military police. The fourth person is the commander of the civilian police, because there are offences committed by the civilian police. The fifth person is the director of the prison, who denounces the facts. And the sixth person is the author of this document. Proceeding in this way, when we look at the document, one finds that the author of the report is calling into question the president of the HVO and the commander of the military police, and he says that the commander of the military police has put himself under the municipal institutions, the president of the HVO, and the brigade commander, and he cites evidence of this, saying that when someone leaves the municipality, he has to have the signature and the stamp of the HVO president. So we are in a very specific situation in Prozor. When we look at this document, one has the impression that the municipal authority in the body of the president of the HVO has an important role and that the commander of the military police has somehow put himself under his orders, but still nothing is being done. Unfortunately, an enormous number of things are taking place, as we see from the document, the looting of convoys, and the commander of the military police says openly that he was authorised to do that, to loot the convoys. The document also says that the military police is participating in combat, so where -- one could understand that they are participating, but then afterwards they engage in criminal activities. That is what this document tells us. And proceeding from that, do you know whether the -- who was the HVO president of Prozor? Was he an individualist, was he someone who did not obey anyone, who had his own policies, or was he closely linked to the civilian structure of the HVO? If you don't know, you tell us that you don't know and I will move on to another question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I will repeat for the hundredth time that the quantity of fighting with the units available while I was there, you will see from the next document that there was so much effort, strength, and energy involved that after at least 20 hours of combat, I would fall into bed, and then the next day things started all over again. I could not do more than I did, and I was responsible for what I did. So you can imagine whatever systems you like. I don't think you can make up a system that does not correspond to reality, but it's up to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have seen a moment ago that counsel for Mr. Coric raised the question, Who were these military police units. But the military police mentioned in this document, in your view, were they people who depended on the chain of command of the military police, with Mr. Coric at the head, or were they people who were in the Rama Brigade and who considered themselves military policemen, they called themselves military policemen, without really being dependent upon Mr. Coric? Do you inform us about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that they belonged to a military police battalion which was within the chain of command of Mr. Coric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I see. So they belonged to a battalion that was within Mr. Coric's chain of command. Very well. You tell us that in the month of August, the situation, in military terms, was so grave that you were concerned solely about the combat and that the military policemen played a role in those operations, so that you didn't concern yourself with all these different aspects. Very well. And Mr. Stringer insists, and he is right, because he wanted you to specify whether you felt responsible for the military police, and my understanding was that your answer was, No, except when they were subordinated to a brigade under my authority. Is that your answer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. So if I analyse this, when they're subordinated to a brigade and they're fighting, in that case, if they commit a crime, you have a role to play. But when they are no longer subordinated and have returned to their houses, or are on leave, or are in a cafe, in such cases you are claiming that you have nothing to do with it, it wasn't a role you had to play?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, the commander is no longer responsible -- well, responsible. If he finds out about something, he'll report it, but then there has to be an investigation carried out by other bodies. It has to be processed by other bodies. He, for example, has to protect a building. But this wasn't possible at the time. Mr. Stringer just wants to have a look at the following document and ask me a few questions about it. He'll see that in such situations, I significantly improved the situation. That was the case wherever I was, I significantly improved the situation. I spoke to people, persuaded them. I prevented the fall of Vakuf, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes before the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Praljak, having listened to you this afternoon, I can recall there was a moment when Mr. Stringer put it to you that you were well aware of the fact that taking away police to the front-line would increase the probability of criminality. You took that in account, you were aware of it, and your point is that this was a case of necessity; that is to say, the situation was so tense that the end of fighting the enemy justified the means of drawing away a police force, which exposed civilians to a greater risk of crime. Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Unfortunately, that was how it was. You have understood my answer correctly. Given what I knew about crime from before, I had lots of information about the criminal law, policemen, and so on and so forth, I'm not stupid. I simply knew that if we reduced the number of military policemen or if -- and that's also what happens when you reduce the number of policemen anywhere in the world, I knew that the result would be that the rate of crime would rise. I was aware of that, Judge Trechsel. The military situation was such that it was necessary to have part of the military police force engaged in battle. I asked for the right for them to be engaged in battle, I was granted this right, and unfortunately that's how it was. I stand by that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, you said that as this was necessary, you sent the military police to the front. But if I deal with Prozor, if you had known about what was happening, about the events described in the document, theft, cases of theft, cases of rape, of arson, attacks launched on convoys, a corrupt military police force, if you had known about all of this, would you have nevertheless said, Well, fine, go into combat, although you knew that having told them to go and fight, the rate of crime was going to rise, because if the military policemen are engaged in combat, they aren't exercising control, the civilian police remain, but they commit crimes, because the document doesn't only concern military policemen; it also concerns civilian police? So if that was the scenario, if you're familiar with this document, for example, would you have sent them into combat in spite of this? The question is difficult. I'm not obliging you to answer the question. You can say, I don't know. But I'm just trying to see how you would have reacted in such a case.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it's a difficult question, Judge Antonetti, it's a very difficult question, but I'll try to answer the question to the best of my ability. At one point in time, it's true that I also assembled the civilian police and went to the front with them because my lines had been broken through. Naturally, just as Vakuf had fallen on the 2nd -- or, rather, between the 1st and 2nd, well, 30 kilometres of my line had fallen. I was returning the line by using a tank and a machine-gun, and I was the first person to do so, I was alone, and then gradually others joined in. The people had fled, the entire population had fled. They had set fire to their own houses, tot warehouses. They blew up the ammunition warehouse. They killed their very own cattle so that the Muslims wouldn't get hold of it. And at such a point in time, in such a situation, having Bugojno in mind, I would probably have sent the police there, in spite of the fact, and then they could have been held to account later. It was a catastrophe that concerned 40.000 individuals. I say that is probably what I -- that is probably what I would have done. I would have sent the police to the front-line in such a situation, too. But when I say "the military police," well, in 1994 - this is something that Colonel Skender will talk about for sure, a high-ranking officer from the Foreign Legion, he will describe the situation to you - but even then, two HVO units were killed, there were two dead individuals, five wounded. I was called in to deal with the situation. We're trying to live in a world which isn't realistic. I was really performing my duties in a courageous manner. It was necessary to be there in the field.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, please complete your questions with the last document before the one-and-only break we will have today.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Is the break at 4.00, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just -- I want to follow up on some of the statements the general's just made in the last few minutes. And if we can put up on the screens in Sanction page 39943 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, General, just a moment ago you were asked by the President about who was responsible for those military police units, and you said that: "I think that they belonged to a military police battalion which was within the chain of command of Mr. Coric." That's page 39, line 10. Now, on the screen, I know you can't read it, this is a transcript from your earlier testimony in this case. This is what you said when you were talking about the same thing. You said: "It is also true ..." This is line 17: "It is also true that due to a heavy offensive on the part of the BH Army, I requested from Mate Boban, and then from Bruno Stojic as well as a body of the second instance, for one part of the military police to be placed at disposal and participate in defence. They still remained military police officers, but in the operative part I was their commander." So, now I know you've just suggested that they were a part of the Coric chain of command, but the fact is, General, that for crimes committed by military police subordinated to you for operational purposes, you, in the operative zone, would be responsible for those crimes and for dealing with those crimes; isn't that true?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it isn't. Operative re-subordination is something I've explained five times already. I don't know how much longer --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So I put it to you that you were aware of those crimes, and are you telling us, General, that even if you were aware that they were committing crimes, you didn't have any responsibility to deal with those perpetrators?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your hypothetical questions are questions I can no longer comment on. Had you known this, had you known that, what would you have done? This is just a matter of speculation, and I don't have an answer to that question. I'll refrain from answering that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, sometimes I also formulate hypotheses. Everyone can do that. The Prosecution is putting a hypothesis to you, says, If you had been aware of crimes at the time, what would you have done? Fine, it's easy to answer. And you answered a conditional question that I previously put to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Antonetti, we dealt with that issue half an hour ago. If I had known about what the document states, I would have told the author of the document to perform his duties. He was responsible to find out who was involved, to report these cases to the prosecution. The individuals in SIS are responsible for security, and the military police should be replaced, they should be taken to prison, and so on and so form. So the person who described these events had the duty of performing his duties, doing his work, not Praljak or anyone else. So it's as if you had an FBI agent who writes to someone else and says, Look, we have some problems, and -- well, the response would be, Well, look, you have to find out who is involved, you have to find evidence, and you have to forward the evidence to the US Attorney's Office so that these individuals can be held to account. We're confusing matters. A policeman drafts a document and says, Listen, I've heard that in the suburbs of Paris, about 100 cars have been set alight. And what then?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I would like to insist a bit on this line. You said you would have told the responsible person to do his duty. Who would that be? Whom would you have told to do his duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] SIS, S-I-S, is responsible for security, the Security Department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you. And while you had taken aware much of the police force, and SIS complained, anyway, that they didn't have the force to do this, how do you think they could have done it? Would you have wondered whether they were able to do the duty you asked them to do, when you had taken away the means they ought to have had at their proposal [sic] to fight crime?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 14th of August, this person stated that the situation had calmed down, and naturally they were already performing their duties again, even if there were certain omissions, because for a period of time they couldn't perform their duties, while subsequently it was possible to arrest and bring in the individuals who had committed the crimes concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Well, that would probably not be very helpful for the victims, but it is -- it is a possible action. I would like to take up the question -- the hypothesis Mr. Antonetti has put to you. Namely, if you had known what was going on behind, not what would you have done; would you have acted in the same way? If you had known more precisely about the crimes that were committed, would you nevertheless have acted the way you have and ordered the police to the front?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I've already answered that question. It's difficult for me to do so, but when confronted with such a situation after the fall of Vakuf and Prozor, if the entire area of Herceg-Bosna was going to have the same fate as Bugojno and Travnik, for example, if the Croats there were going to have the same fate, it's very probable that I would have done the same thing. I would assembled everyone who could bear arms in order to prevent the area from falling, because I was a commander and the main task of a commander is to prevent defeat from occurring, which would lead his army and people - and there had been other examples in Konjic, in Travnik, in Bugojno before that – into a situation involving hundreds of dead, people who had been expelled, and so on and so forth. Therefore, Judge Trechsel, even if I had been aware of certain facts, it's very probable that I would have acted in the same manner. I wouldn't want to lie to you. I'm telling you that it's highly probable, not to say certain, because one can never claim for certain what one would have done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Praljak. It seems today we have better relations than on other days, because again you have satisfied my question, you really answered my question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge Trechsel, I always want to answer your questions. Misunderstandings don't occur because I want to muddy the water, but this has been going on for so long that it's inevitable for certain misunderstandings to occur. It's not that I want misunderstandings to occur.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
