utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have our break now, because we will be running out of tape. We'll have a 20-minute break, and we will then resume at 4.20. The hearing will come to an end at 1800 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I apologise. I was just trying to clarify the next exhibit to make sure it's available to everyone. Mr. President, we've been talking extensively about P034 -- sorry, 4177, and over the break I reached the conclusion that from the Prosecution point of view, we've exhausted the issues that the document raises and that I'm prepared to move on to the next topic, the next -- which is one of the documents that we passed over yesterday. So I'd like to come back to a document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, it's 3D00484, and this -- General, I think you'll recognise, it's one of your document. This is a report that you talked about during your examination, your direct. Do you recognise this, General, as the report made by Ante Prkacin about his efforts to reach the Jajce front-line in October 1992?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And for the record, Mr. President, the -- and I think the Praljak Defence team will agree with me, it seemed to us that the initial translation that had been made, I understand, quite a long time ago by the Praljak Defence was not a great one, and so we've had the document re-translated, and so there's a new version which was distributed in hard copy to everyone yesterday, and also to the Trial Chamber as well. And I'm told that it is in e-court, or if it's not in e-court yet, it's in the process, but just to make sure we're on the same version, Mr. President, the translation now is one that's double-spaced, and up in the upper right-hand corner it says "ET 3D19-0240." So just to make sure we're on the correct translation, not the old one, because the translation that's on the screen is not the correct one. So the correct one is not yet in e-court. So if it's agreeable to everyone, I can continue with the document and we can just work on the hard copy, since we can't get -- okay. Actually, we can put it up in Sanction, the correct translation or the new translation, so we can have it on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, I want to take you back to an earlier part of your testimony. This is page 41851 of the transcript, and this is your evidence from the 23rd of June of this year. And you spoke about the fall of Jajce, and there's -- your testimony on the fall of Jajce is something I want to challenge you on, and I want to challenge you with this particular report of Mr. Prkacin. So let me take you back and read to you a part of your testimony from June about the fall of Jajce. You said: "Jajce fell into Serb hands. A unit comes from Croatia, about 270 strong, and it comprises 80 per cent Muslims and 20 per cent Croats, and they have volunteered to assist in the defence of Jajce." And then I'm going to skip down a few lines. You say: "So this joint unit, with this ethnic composition, didn't manage to reach Central Bosnia, Travnik, because the Muslim units and the Muslim politicians prevented it from getting there. They spent three days on a bus from Gornji Vakuf to Travnik. They were mistreated, weapons were trained on them, and so forth, and I claim that this marked the beginning of an organised preparation on the part of the BH Army and some of the people in the SDA leadership for the future conquest of Central Bosnia." And then again skipping down a few lines: "It was a terrible, terrible knowledge, it was quite surprising, and it really reflected the trends in the Muslim military and politics in the time that followed. That's what I'm claiming." So now, General, I want to challenge that testimony by going through Mr. Prkacin's report with you of the events, his trip trying to get from Grude to Jajce which, as he indicates here, began on the 28th of October, 1992. Now, you'll see, right at the very beginning of the document, the second sentence, he says: "The first trouble, though not a major one, happened at a check-point seven to eight kilometres between Tomislavgrad and Prozor, when the HVO military police would not accept our pass, i.e., a signed order, approved by Mr. Petkovic, HVO chief of staff. They demanded and we counted and listed -- they demanded that we counted and listed the soldiers. One of the soldiers asked me, 'Are there any balijas? I'll kill them all.' Given the composition of this unit, the question was quite awkward." And then he goes on to talk about how he was -- Prkacin was able to resolve the situation there and pass through this check-point. Now, before moving on, General, as you indicated in your testimony, it is true that this group of soldiers that Prkacin was taking up to Jajce was mostly constituted of Muslims; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think that 80 per cent of them were Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: All right. And this being a group of HVO -- an HVO group of soldiers, mostly Muslims, with Ante Prkacin, General, is this a group of soldiers that had recently come across to the HVO from the HOS, which Mr. Prkacin had been associated with in the months previous?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were mostly volunteers from Croatia, the people that Mr. Prkacin brought with him, volunteers from Croatia, HOS. They didn't join the HVO, they remained HOS members, and among them, about 80 per cent of them were Muslims, and in Capljina they were reinforced with what was lacking and went off towards Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So moving down a few lines, then, Prkacin reports: "We arrived in Prozor only around 0700 hours, due to extremely difficult driving conditions." And as he indicates there, he contacted Glasnovic and two additional groups, and that 30 men, anti-terrorist platoon from Siroki Brijeg, and others were waiting for him. And then he says they waited around two hours until the guys got ready, and they were looking for a vehicle to transport the 20 men. So then he reports that they started moving toward Vakuf at around 2000 hours, with the police at the head. And then he says they reached Bugojno, where control was carried out jointly between HVO military police and the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. Here he says the HVO let them pass, but the BH Army asked for a written request for passage in order to respond to it in writing. And then the next paragraph, he talks about meeting with the ABiH commander there, Mr. Sead Dautovic, who received him warmly but asked for a list of soldiers and officers. And you can see in the text that follows Prkacin resisted providing that information. And then in the lines that follow here, he talks about Dautovic then contacting Mr. Lendo, who I think you referred to in your testimony at one point. And ultimately Prkacin was issued a pass, but he said it was rather bizarre because they were going to have a police escort and they were also being escorted by an anti-terrorist group who was to protect them, but in the event of them lining their troops in a suspicious manner, to destroy them. Prkacin says he accepted this almost unconditionally because he wanted to reach Jajce as soon as possible, but the HVO police members' reaction was strong. They said it was unacceptable. And so he's describing the difficulties or the tensions that resulted from this -- the conditions that came with this HVO pass. And then he talks about being in Bugojno, at the headquarters in Bugojno, the military police, Mr. Suvalic and Mr. Bilos, and they didn't like the situation, if I can put it that way. And he refers then to an anti-terrorist group from Siroki Brijeg, 30 strong, and he says: "There was another such group in my unit whose commander came to me to ask for a permission to attack the BH Army members who encircled us. Predrag Mandic (Lija) leader of the Siroki Brijeg group did a similar thing, telling me he was ready, so when I felt the moment was right, give him a signal." And it's at this point Prkacin says he ordered them to turn around and go back to Bugojno until the HVO and the ABiH could reach an agreement about passage. And then he says they returned to Bugojno and the joint representatives of the BH Army, Dautovic, and the HVO, Zivko, came along and reached agreement and ready to let us pass. This came after five hours of waiting. Prkacin talks about how it was getting tense or edgy, and then he says: "The Siroki Brijeg commander, Mandic, was categorical, he said, 'I am for fighting and I am not afraid to die, but this is a suicide mission without brains. Tuta (his superior officer Tuta Naletilic) ordered me to use my judgement well before I went anywhere, so my judgement is that this is useless and too dangerous, and so I'm going back ...'." Just one question on this, General. Is that consistent with your knowledge at the time, October 1992, that Predrag Mandic was a subordinate of Mladen Naletilic, Tuta?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't say. It's not a question I can answer with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: That's fine. I don't want you to speculate. If you don't know, I can accept that.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I'm afraid that you have skipped many things in this document. It's the sabotage part of the ABiH escorting the convoy. They took out Zoljas and pointed them at the convoy. They surrounded them. There were 20 young men trained in Split among them, and they had been born in Central Bosnia. They went to assist them up there. I stand by my testimony --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, no, you're right, I'm not going to read the entire document because we're going to be here for the rest of the day. I'm trying to read parts of it. Everyone can read the document in its entirety. I'm trying to get through this so that we can get a general overview of where they were and what happened. And it's clear, as we move through this, I think everyone is seeing that there are a number of things happening that are causing a lot of tension as they continue on. Now, so let me just continue with this. What he says is that they reached an agreement in Bugojno and they were ready to leave. Now I'm at page 3 of the -- the top of page 3 of the English version. And then he says that just as they were getting ready to go, the BH Army would not allow the passage along the route just agreed, but then proposed an original -- or an alternative route via Vakuf-Pavlovica. And then he goes on and he talks about having passed a few barricades without difficulty. He says they reached the Sebesic check-point, where the commanding officer was Ivica Cobanac, whose men expressed huge opposition toward the Muslims: "... which was an additional upset for the Muslims in my unit. I went with Mr. Cobanac to his office. He promised to let the convoy through, despite the fact that he hated the Turks more than the Serbs because they had killed more of his men than the Chetniks, but he claimed that we would not get safe passage at the next two semi-private Muslim barricades because those were also Croat-haters and criminals, so he proposed to clear the way with hand held anti-tank rocket-launchers and RPGs." Now, General, what we did not do -- perhaps I should have done at the beginning of this. We're talking about the 28th of October 1992. We're talking about a period of time where this unit is attempting to pass through areas which are very close to the Prozor area, in which combat activities between the ABiH and the HVO have been taking place for several days; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, this is about Bugojno and the area between Bugojno and Travnik. Prozor, in spite of this, had allowed all those volunteer units to pass to assist in the joint defence of Jajce, though it was about to fall.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: My point is this: that because of the events in Prozor at this very same time that are clearly going to be known to HVO and ABiH in other areas in the region, there's a tremendous amount tension and suspicion and fear at all of the -- along all of the routes and all the check-points; correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The HVO let them pass, regardless of Cobanac. He experienced a total massacre by the Mujahedin, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, then: If the ABiH, based on the events that were taking place in Prozor, was hesitant about letting a well-armed, large group or groups of HVO soldiers move through its territory, they would have been justified, wouldn't they?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, these are Muslims, and if they won't let them pass, how can a unit, composed 80 per cent of Muslims, how could it have been used in any way against the Muslims of Bosnia and Herzegovina? This is not correct. This is an indicator of what I said. Already then, the Army of Bosnia- Herzegovina considered the HVO something that they would need to defeat in the future. To accept 200 Muslims in the unit, and there were at least 200 of them, this could only have benefitted them to show that HVO who led the team had no ethnic divisions and they wanted jointly to fight in Jajce, so they didn't send such aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What we've seen so far is that at two of these check-points, in fact, the ethnic composition of this group raised a hostility among the HVO. They didn't want to -- you know, they didn't want to let balijas through, they didn't want to let Turks through. They did so reluctantly, but this certainly contributed to delay and suspicion, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is true that there were individuals of this type, but the HVO succeeded to force such individuals to let the convoy pass, and it did. But the HVO or General Petkovic didn't provide an escort with -- of anti-terrorist teams with trained weapons. An individual is an individual, and the position of the command, which is being implemented even with difficulty, is something else. This was the position of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and in our case it was only individuals. Even the position of Cobanac, that the ABiH army had killed more of his men, which is true, is one thing, but he says, I let them pass, because he received such an order. But those over there will not let you pass, because the next team were Mujahedin at Rostovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So what Prkacin talks about is moving up to those next Muslim barricades, and I'm not going to read all of this, but essentially he talks about the thoughts that were racing through his head and what should he do. And so I'm skipping now down toward the bottom of page 3 of the English. He says that he decided and ordered that they go back. It says: "... deep in a forest, on a bad forest-path and heavy rain, tried to find billeting in Bugojno or Vakuf through the police, but they would not even allow us to park the buses; rather, they escorted us to Prozor, where we arrived well after midnight. We were not able to arrange billeting there, so the men were sleeping on the buses." Now, General, so Prkacin arrives back in Prozor, and he's not even able to find a place for these people to sleep. The next morning, on the 29th, they reassemble, and he says now they were joined by a platoon of BH Army from Mostar, and they received firm guarantees that they would be escorted by a joint police escort to Travnik, to a large barracks where the men can rest and eat after 60 tiring hours. And he says then: "This time we managed to reach Travnik, despite minor difficulties (a few delays in some places, a truck deliberately left across the road by the Muslims in the village of Opare) ..." So they meet up with this BH Army platoon, they receive a joint police escort and are able to pass from Prozor all the way to Travnik on the 29th of October, and then he talks about what happened after they arrived there. He went to see Colonel Blaskic. Again, he's trying to find billeting, a place for these guys to sleep. He's making proposals so that they can rest up before moving to the front-line. And he says: "They agreed to that. Blaskic selected Mr. Filipovic to go with me to Travnik to follow this through. But Mr. Filipovic failed in this. Instead of issuing decisive orders, he begged and proposed, and that brought no results." So now these units with Prkacin are in the Central Bosnia Operative Zone. The operative zone commander turns them over to Filipovic to find accommodation so they can rest, and the HVO can't even find beds for these people. He continues, he says: "The officers of the ABiH promised to help with billeting the men in a room with no beds, but this had poor results. They managed to free up only one room, with no beds or covers, so most of the men remained on the bus." And then he continues on, General. Skipping down a paragraph, he says: "After we left Travnik, heading towards Turbe, our vehicle was fired upon from light infantry weapons." I'm going to move to the next page in the English. He talks about the events and his observations when he was trying to get to Jajce to see what the situation was out there, and he says: "We also saw a number of civilians and soldiers walking towards Travnik." Do you see that part, General?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see them walking towards Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: "At Karaula, we encountered obstructions which were set up so as to prevent the passage of vehicles towards Jajce." And he talks about all that and basically says that after all that -- after that: " ... on both sides of the road, so we had to give up on the attempt to get to Jajce. Instead, we returned to Travnik, presented all we saw to the Command of ABiH (because we could not find the HVO members) and we suggested to them to clear up the road. They promised to do so, but they did not succeed in that because we had tried again around 3.00 or 4.00 p.m., but we failed again. We managed to do something else. By now, we were seeing a very big number of soldiers moving in a disorderly fashion from Jajce towards Travnik. Through conversations with some of them, we found out that our side (HVO and ABiH) were completely deserting also the flank lines." And he goes on to talk about various things they tried to do to deal with the situation. And then at the very end, he concludes: "I think that Jajce should serve as our last lesson and a warning. We cannot win this war by leading such a battle with such an enemy. Being engaged in a defence war does not at the same time mean exclusively defending oneself. We must give up on the trench-based battles ..." And he continues on. So, General, I realise I've taken some time to go through this document, and I also realise I haven't read it to you in its entirety - everybody can do that - but I'm going to put to you, General, that your testimony about the fall of Jajce and blaming it on the ABiH or Muslim political goals is not true, and in fact what we know from this account is that the ABiH and the HVO, soldiers and units on check-points and in all of this terrain, all of this tension and difficulty contributed to the fact that those soldiers did not reach Jajce and that the fall of Jajce is not something that is a result of profound political wish or desire on the part of the Muslim leadership. So I'm putting that to you. Would you agree with me on that?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't need to agree with you because I didn't say anywhere, as far as I can recollect, that the fall of Jajce was caused by this kind of behaviour towards the general of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Ante Prkacin. He's a general of the ABiH. Jajce fell for quite different reasons that I didn't delve into. I don't think you can find in any part of my testimony that I accused the politicians for the loss of Jajce or that I linked the fall of Jajce to this event. I spoke about this event from a completely different standpoint, and that is that the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina showed an unbelievable behaviour towards a unit of 200 and odd troops, 80 per cent of whom were Muslims who wanted to assist. The fall of Jajce may have happened or not even if it had been different, but such behaviour in -- at a time of joint defence shows that there were cracks already at a very high level, not at the individual level.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, I read your testimony -- I read to you your testimony earlier about this, in fact, when you did link the fall of Jajce with political objectives of the Muslims. Let me read it to you again. This is again from page 41851. You say: "And I claim that this marked the beginning of an organised preparation on the part of the BH Army and some people in the SDA leadership for future conquest of Central Bosnia, because how can you trust somebody's good intentions about the joint fight if such a unit, after the fall of Jajce, is not allowed to pass through to Jajce at any cost? It was a terrible, terrible knowledge, it was quite surprising, and it really reflected the trends in the Muslim military and politics in the time that followed. That's what I'm claiming." General, what I'm claiming is that, based on this report, what we see is that Prkacin wasn't able to get --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: What I'm claiming is that, as we see from this report, there are a good many factors on the HVO and the ABiH side that resulted in delays, and a conflict situation, a tense conflict situation, and that one simply can't ascribe the fall of Jajce or the failure of Prkacin to get to Jajce on time. You can't simply lay that at the feet of one side of this conflict. That's what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would be grateful if you were to read where I said that the fall of Jajce was linked to this. I was talking about the period after the fall of Jajce and my thoughts about it. I was quite right, my assessments were correct. All my efforts to prevent those assessments from coming true, and these efforts went on until the month of May 1993, unfortunately were in vain, and I fully stand by my testimony, which is precise, and I did not link the fall of Jajce to the arrival of this unit, as you are claiming.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Mr. President, I'm ready to move to the next binder and the next topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, I have two questions. The first is quite simple, and the second will be more complicated. The first is that, on the basis of this document, we see that there's an incident at this check-point. We have seen numerous documents referring to check-points. A few days ago, we had a document of Mr. Petkovic which insisted on the need to ensure this control, and I have been thinking about this for some time. Could you tell me if, in the JNA doctrine, the little you know about it because it is of a highly military nature, in the ex-Yugoslavia the JNA doctrine and the doctrine of the Yugoslav generals, was it to control, within the territory of ex-Yugoslavia, all the communication routes with the help of check-points, in view of the topography? By having control, this would ensure this Chinese Communist concept of people's defence, all people's Defence. Therefore, in ex-Yugoslavia, and specifically in the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina, did the check-points correspond to a military strategy whereby one controlled the movement of enemy troops? This is a rather simple question, but of a military nature. Could you answer it, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. According to what I know, but -- well, not only in the JNA, but in all armies, the military police has the duty of controlling roads at certain check-points. They have to control the movement of convoys, soldiers, and in this way they have an overview of the situation and they prevent military unacceptable acts from occurring. That's what I have learnt from the various literature, from films. In each and every war, military check-points are set up at which vehicles are controlled in areas that are affected by war, and our area was affected by a war. This is what I know about the matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Another question that relates to check-points. We've seen numerous documents which show that there were incidents at check-points on occasion. That was the case here. We've seen in certain documents that some, on both sides, HVO -- the HVO and the ABiH, they imposed taxes when people or vehicles wanted to pass through the check-points. This was perhaps not authorised. As far as you know, was this a system that was necessary, that was organised, or was this just a matter of the individual behaviour of certain soldiers who are manning the check-points? Did they just say that they would combine business and pleasure and impose taxes, levy taxes on those who were passing through the check-points?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the so-called irregular [as interpreted] check-points set up at certain locations and controlled by the military police, there were occasionally check-points that had been set up by a brigade. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I apologise. We have an important error in the transcript. It's page 63, line 6. General Praljak said "apart from regular check-points," whereas the transcript says the contrary, it says "apart from the irregular check-points." I think this is very important, and it would be good for Mr. Praljak to repeat what he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please repeat what you said.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the regular check-points, HVO or ABiH check-points manned above all by the military police, there were occasionally other check-points. The commander, when his unit was passing through or returning from the battle-field, the commander would establish a check-point and check whether everyone had passed through, and so on and so forth. But, Your Honours, the number of wild check-points was just too great. After Prkacin, I passed through Central Bosnia, and I think I was stopped at least 15 times by incredible individuals, and it's only as a theatre director, as an actor, that I was able to pass through. I had to assess how to behave towards these individuals, and I could give you an example of what individuals had to do in order to pass through. Sometimes they would be there for two days. They'd steal some things, then move on to another location and then disappear. They'd just come out onto the road, set up a few stones or rocks and some kind of -- and a few pieces of wood, they'd have their weapons with them, and then you had to stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that answer. And now for my second question, which is somewhat complicated. I've been listening to you for several weeks now, and on a number of occasions you've spoken about Jajce, well known for its waterfalls, if I'm not mistaken. And towards the end of the afternoon, Mr. Stringer has shown you a document on Jajce. He put questions to you about the link between an Izetbegovic action, Muslim actions, and the fall of Jajce. Let's try and see things clearly. You said that in Jajce, there were Muslims and the HVO facing the Serbs. They were at the front-line, and then things exploded, units left. It was quite a catastrophe, it would appear, because many refugees left, and it seems that 20.000 Muslim refugees left in all directions. I say this with caution. Did the fact that there were refugees pose a double problem to Izetbegovic, in that they had to be provided with accommodation, that they had to go somewhere? And then, secondly, was he going to use them within the framework of what we call the Vance-Owen Plan? It would appear to demonstrate that Izetbegovic was taking advantage of the situation that there were thousands of people on the road, the HVO had certainly been weakened in the course of this route, and at that point in time he may have planned an attack, together with Halilovic and others, that was to be launched against the HVO, and this might, in a certain manner, explain the events that transpired in Prozor. So there might be a link. There was Jajce, the refugees, taking political and military advantage of the situation by Halilovic and Izetbegovic, and then the events in Prozor. Is this possible or not? What would you say? I'm putting this question to you, General Praljak, because pursuant to the provisions of the Statute, the Judges at the end of the trial have to rule on whether you are guilty or innocent, and part of their mission is to state what actually happened, in a judgement. It is therefore necessary, in one way or another, to explain how all these events occurred. I personally need to put such questions and receive appropriate answers to try and understand what exactly took place. So I'm presenting you with an event that may have occurred. You can say, It's true, It's not true, and you can tell me what the reason is for your answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I fail to see a causal link between the fall of Jajce and the events in Prozor. I don't think there is any such link, to answer the first part of your question. Muslims and Croats lived in Jajce. The ABiH and the HVO was defending Jajce. Perhaps HVO troops were somewhat more numerous than ABiH troops. Jajce fell. In my opinion, given the way it was defended, it couldn't defend itself, in military terms, because from Travnik to Jajce there was an area controlled by the Serbs, so providing supplies was difficult because you could see Prkacin said that they were firing at a distance of 200 metres from the road. The stretch that I mentioned where I tried to do something was completely under the control Army of Republika Srpska. In military terms, Jajce would have fallen five days earlier or five days later. Given the military situation at the time, it was impossible to prevent. Then Croatian refugees arrived, and many of the HVO members from Jajce passed through. They stopped in Croatia, Makarska, et cetera, and they also asked for their salaries to be paid. The Jajce Brigade, the Muslims from the ABiH, instead of acting logically and going to Tuzla, in the direction of Srebrenica and Sarajevo, moved to Gornji Vakuf, where there was no danger from the Army of Republika Srpska, and there they provoked the next disturbances. Why move a brigade to Vakuf, whereas you are fighting against the Serbs who are not present in Gornji Vakuf? And the line held by the armija towards good positions is a short one. And the refugees, Muslims on the whole, remain in Vakuf, the majority of them in Travnik, and the ethnic composition of the population significantly changes. There are naturally -- there are problems, requests that start to lead to changes in the opinions or positions of the political leadership. Because of that energy, those people have new requests. They become aware of the fact that they won't be returning to areas where Serbs are present. They don't believe in a just solution. They are trying to find territory for themselves by having recourse to various means. They are bitter, they are tired, they've been driven out, they've been killed. It's a powder keg, one powder keg next to another. There's a lot of energy present. There are people who no longer trust anyone in the world. They're trying to find an area for themselves, and the policies pursued in the field have to adapt to the situation so that the people can be provided with accommodation. And the HVO and the Croat believe that -- well, Look, there were 50 per cent of us or 40 per cent of us here yesterday, now we 7 per cent or 20 per cent, we represent 7 or 20 per cent, and so on and so forth. So that's how things start developing, and then significant events occur. Why not let through such a unit because it's not just a matter of Jajce now. Travnik has no defence. There's nothing as far as Sarajevo. Why not let them through so that lines are established, because you have seen the power that Filipovic had up by the barracks and the ABiH commanders, naturally, and at that point, Your Honours, naturally I took over responsibility for commanding Travnik, for digging trenches, for defending that area, and so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. General Praljak, thank you. It was a long answer, but I draw two conclusions from what you have said. First of all, there is no link with the events in Prozor, and, secondly, you say the following, and this seems to be important to me. It's for everyone to assess. These refugees modified the ethnic composition of the places, and you say that in certain places there were 40 per cent of Croats and then the percentage could fall to 7 per cent, for example. So I'll bear this in mind and reflect on the matter at a later stage. Very well. I will now give the floor back to Mr. Stringer. Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Please, bear the following in account -- take the following into account. Then people started having more radical ideas. Those who had more radical solutions were more acceptable than those who were saying how things should be calmed down. Unfortunately, that was the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please do hurry up, and we will distribute the new binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Stringer, will we have a new binder? I'm looking for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: It's the binder called "List Number 7." And, in fact, while the general is taking his quick break, maybe the usher could take number 6 away so that binder 7 is ready when he comes back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: General, the next binder has been put on the table in front of you there. We're going to move forward in time -- or we're going to move now to discuss the situation in Gornji Vakuf. If you would turn to the first exhibit, P00643. General, this is dated 24th of October, 1992, from Commander Colonel Siljeg. It's a command for action. General, as I understand, on the 24th of October, 1992, you had not yet arrived in this area, in the Prozor area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct, I hadn't arrived.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Were you aware -- did you become aware that Colonel Siljeg had issued a command for action, directing that -- I'll just read it: "Put the town under your control." This is to the HVO Ante Starcevic Brigade, Gornji Vakuf: "Put the town under your control. Control all routes and fiercely prevent any attack on the HVO units." Were you aware that Colonel Siljeg issued this command prior to your arrival in the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't aware that he had done this. This was for Ante Starcevic in Gornji Vakuf.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's go to the next document, and then I'll ask a couple of questions about both of these. The next one is P00460. And, General, the form of this one is a bit unusual. You'll see, I believe, that it appears to be --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not 460. Which one is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: P00460. You should have 460 in your binder.

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's right. I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: And what you're going to see is on the original version it appears we've got two separate packet communications that are appearing on this one page, and I'm only interested in the first one, the one on top, which is dated "27.10," which we take to be the 27th of October, and this is a 1992 document, we see from the upper left-hand side. General, in this one Colonel Siljeg is calling this an urgent report requested, and he's directing this to brigades in Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor, and he says: "We immediately request information on the situation in Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor. Provide estimate of a possibility of passage on the roads ..." And then he says: "Provide estimate of a possibility of eliminating the Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf." And then he's asking if they've established a connection with Major Jure Smidt and what the result are. Now, General, this is the 27th of October. The previous document is the 24th of October. Both of these documents -- well, let me ask you first: The second document that we've just looked at now, were you aware of this order or request from Siljeg to provide an estimate of the possibility of eliminating the Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf, were you aware of this document when you arrived in the North-West Herzegovina Operative Zone?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, let me just continue. Can we agree, General, that both of these orders were issued prior to the fall of Jajce, as indicated in the report of Mr. Prkacin that we've just gone through?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that Jajce fell on the 27th or the 28th. It depends what you consider a fall, whether when it was all the refugees had fall -- had left or when all the front-lines had been broken through. So it depends.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Now, just a few moments ago, and I'm looking at page 66 of today's transcript, line 14, you said: "Why move a brigade to Vakuf?" You were talking about the ABiH, and why would they move a brigade to Vakuf after the fall of Jajce, rather than moving a brigade somewhere else, such as Tuzla. My question is -- on that, General, is this, I'll suggest this to you: After the fall of Jajce, the ABiH was required or had to send a brigade down to Vakuf, if in fact that's what they did, in order to deal with these sorts of actions and attempts by the HVO to take the town of Gornji Vakuf under control; isn't that why the ABiH would have had to send one of its brigades to Vakuf?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARNAVAS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object. It calls for speculation. He obviously cannot know what they had in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, the general said he's attributed improper motives to the ABiH, saying they should have done this, they should have done that, they should have sent a brigade somewhere else. Now, I think it's fair to use these documents to suggest to the general that they were, in fact, legitimate reasons.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, General Praljak can answer, or he can say, I can't answer. If he can, it can contribute to the establishment of the truth. If not, he can say that, I didn't know of the existence of this document and I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours and Mr. Stringer, this is an order for action, not an order for attack, and it says clearly: "Liberate the communication in Gornji Vakuf to Prozor. Eliminate all attacks on HVO units." So the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina has already intercepted communication. The army does not allow the commander of the brigade in Vakuf to reach his premises. So when it says to put the town under control, it's not conquer the town, it's prevent, and eliminate, by your deployment, so that HVO units should not be attacked, and see if you can liberate -- open the communication, the routes to Gornji Vakuf, Bugojno, et cetera. Otherwise, how will Merhamet pass, which is carrying weapons for the Muslims, if the roads are blocked, which is what the next document will tell you, signed by Susak or Praljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The fact is just prior to the fall of Jajce, Siljeg is issuing orders to his brigades to provide to him an estimate of the possibility of eliminating Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf, so clearly he's thinking about operations to eliminate the ABiH forces in Vakuf. So if that's the case, then that's a legitimate reason for the ABiH to respond by sending a brigade down there, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: So they should --

utterances.speaker: SLOBODAN PRALJAK [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is an estimate of the possibility of eliminating after he says there can be no passage along the roads Prozor-Vakuf-Bugojno-Travnik. So the aggression has already started, but not by the HVO. And he says, If we cannot pass along that route, then of course --

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's move forward in time and to the next document, P01068.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we see the next document, I should like to go back to the first document. I see a military document, and I'm trying to analyse it from a military standpoint. Colonel Siljeg is sending to the Ante Starcevic Brigade a document, an order, saying, Put the town under your control, control all the routes, and he adds, and I think this is important, in order to prevent an attack on HVO units. Therefore, in military terms, General Praljak, could it be, because unfortunately the persons writing these documents are not present - normally one would have reviewed all this, and here this is not possible, so we're forced to make hypotheses - is it possible that Colonel Siljeg had information on the basis of which there was a possibility of an attack on the HVO, and in order to counter this - I'm not saying to attack - but to counter it, the first military step that he is ordering is to control the routes? In military terms, is that a possibility or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just a technical point. It does not say, at least in the translation, but I think the translation on this point is correct, it's says not "in order to prevent any attack," but "and prevent any attack," so that it is put one next to the other and not one as a means to achieve the other.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the document, in B/C/S, could you read the sentence? What exactly does it say?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Put the town under your control. Control the communications and resolutely eliminate any attack against HVO units. Be in touch with HVO brigade, the Eugen Kvaternik HVO Brigade in Bugojno, and the Rama HVO Brigade in Prozor. Establish mutual communication and, if possible, jointly free the route between Gornji Vakuf and Prozor."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] General Praljak, as my colleague has said, there are two things to be done; control the roads and eliminate all attacks against the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct, but to put the town under your control does not mean to capture it militarily, but where important facilities exist, place the HVO on the ready and prevent and repulse any attack against HVO units. And the communications between Vakuf and Rama has already been blocked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will move on to the second document immediately. Could we not read it to say that Colonel Siljeg is asking Eugen Kvaternik Brigade and the other brigades, because you see the difference between the documents is that the first is addressed only to one brigade, whereas the second is addressed to three brigades, and he is requesting an assessment of the situation; that is, the possibility of passage on the roads and the possibility of eliminating Muslim forces in Gornji Vakuf, and to establish connection with Jure Smidt, and he's waiting for the results? The second argument: Is it a request to assess the possibility without containing an order for an attack, or is this an order for an attack?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There's no attack. He's asking for a report. He's saying, Provide an estimate of a possibility of passage, which means that there is no passage, the roads are blocked. And any normal commander would say, Give us an assessment of the forces which we may attack if we fail to de-block the entire HVO of Central Bosnia. Then that is a war. But the war was not started by the HVO, but by the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina by blocking all the roads.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My last question. If I proceed from the hypothesis that Colonel Siljeg had decided to attack, to take control of Gornji Vakuf, to take prisoners, et cetera, wouldn't there then be quite a different order, the classical type of order with item 1, 2, 3, The attack will begin at such and such a time, report about progress? Would one not have such a classical type of order?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. You have seen what attack orders look like, but I assure you, Your Honours, that in the following days talks in Rama, Bugojno, Gornji Vakuf and Travnik, I managed to deal with the situation. The roads were much freer, the situation calmed down, Travnik was defended, and until the 11th of January, 1993, the situation was more or less decent and -- in terms of relations between the two parties, because I went to the front-lines of the ABiH, I saw their commanders, and we planned joint actions, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: A question of logic to you, Mr. Praljak. It says here: "We urgently request information...," inter alia, of a possibility of passage on the roads. The rest is not relevant. You have affirmed that this means that there is no passage, and I do not understand how you interpret a request for information as meaning that there is a certain answer already at hand. I'm referring to page 74, line 21, which is doomed to pass from our view, full stop.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The sentence, in my view, is a logical one. He's asking for an assessment of the possibility of passage. In other words, as talks went on in Bugojno, Travnik, whether those talks - this is in my view because I am aware that there were such talks - would this lead to the de-blocking of the roads, which actually happened later on? So give us an assessment of this possibility means how are those talks progressing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to tell that Praljak, when he was mentioning that communication is not open, he was referring on the document 460, where it is clear from the last sentence, while the one you were talking now -- sorry, sorry, I mixed the document. It is in 643, in the first document, last sentence. In it, he says that the communication is not open, and this is what Mr. Praljak was referring. And the second document, 460, is having the sentence you were discussing, you and Mr. Praljak. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you, yes, and 460 is a few days later, so -- but, I mean, I think we have clearly the question, we have an answer. It's not for me, at this moment, to comment, and I think we can proceed. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I just wanted to say that when -- Mr. Praljak, before your question, like one page before, when he said that he understood the road is closed, he understood it from the document which was prepared on 24 October. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I find it amazing that you know so exactly what the witness is meaning. I think it's for him to interpret what he means, and not for his lawyers to say what he is saying or what he meant to say. But I think we should -- we should leave it at that and continue now. This is not a very fruitful exchange. It's not unpleasant, but neither does it add much to the task of this Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, I apologise. I simply wanted to be helpful, because Praljak said so like two minutes before you asked, because he was referring to this document. That was obvious. But -- and I read the document carefully, both of -- and, I'm sorry, I wanted to help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Mr. Kovacic, your candid intentions are not questioned. Mr. Stringer.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Let's just move to the next document, General, P01068. 01068. General, this is a report of the British Battalion. It's dated 6th of January, 1993, so it's later in time, and it is relating to the situation in Gornji Vakuf on that day. And you've just been talking about the roads and the situation involving control of the roads, and I know you've been claiming that the ABiH has been cutting -- or had cut off the roads -- or certain roads in this area, forcing the HVO commander to use the UNPROFOR to get to his headquarters. Here, in the second paragraph, it says, on the third line: "Comment: There is an earth-work barrier at this check-point in order to force the Muslim population of Hare to travel to Prozor and not Gornji Vakuf. Obviously, tensions are rising in the area, which is reflected by an HVO presence at the check-point." Then the next paragraph says: "At approximately 1500 hours on Monday afternoon, the HVO raised an Ustasha flag in the town. The Muslims reacted and a Bosnian Army soldier attempted to remove the flag. An HVO policeman then fired at the Bosnian Army soldier ..." I'm not going to continue with my questioning, Mr. President, until all the distracting discussion in the courtroom stops. I mentioned it yesterday. It's -- I don't think Mr. Kovacic understands how well his baritone voice carries, and it's really hard to concentrate when there's constant conversation coming from that side of the room. I'm sure he's got a lovely singing voice, but it really does carry.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise, I'm sorry. I was not aware of that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Praljak.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have never so far made such a request, but this is my 58th day. Could we perhaps stop 15 minutes earlier today, Mr. Stringer, and then we could continue later? I'm somewhat exhausted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak, we were to end this hearing at 6.00 p.m. today. I know you are tired; I, too. Everyone, in fact, here is tired. All the documents require one to pay a lot of attention to them. When I ask questions, I have to be very careful. It's very stressful, because I have to be very careful about how I formulate my questions, and as a result the nervous tension is immense. And as a result, I am completely exhausted at the end of the hearing. I put myself in your shoes, and I believe that you, too, find yourself in the same situation because you wonder whether there are any traps hidden behind certain questions. If you would like us to stop here, I don't see why not, because I have said if you want to finish, we can finish. Fifteen minutes isn't that important. I believe that my colleagues are in agreement with that. Mr. Stringer, we will continue with the binder next Monday. How many more binders will follow? I thought there were a few.

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: Well, at this moment, Your Honour, there is only one, but there will be more by Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, that's what I wanted to know. How many binders do you still have?

utterances.speaker: MR. STRINGER
utterances.text: The binders haven't been made yet. I can tell Your Honour that in terms of the issues that raise, because we're putting issues in binders - I think that we have issues relating to camps, in general - there will be documents on what we're alleging is the arrest campaign of the summer of 1993, and events in Southern Herzegovina, Capljina, Stolac. There is going to be documentation regarding the town of Mostar, and then some additional -- and fewer documents relating to such things as Vares. And I think as I indicated in our filing from before, we're probably going to come back briefly to international armed conflict and also some questions on it related to cooperation issues with the VRS. So I think there are four or five issues that remain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I see that you still have a certain number of binders to deal with. Very well. Mr. Praljak, we will stop here, and we'll see each other again next Monday. Have a good rest in the meantime, and I wish everyone a good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to thank Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
